question: The Times Square ball drop copies an old harbour device. Every day, a ball dropped from a tower at an exact time. Who was it for?
source_excerpt: Time balls were built so navigators could check their marine chronometers against a reliable time reference.

extra.why_interesting: Players think of the ball drop as pure party showmanship. In fact it copies a practical device built so sailors could set their clocks, which turns a TV spectacle into a piece of navigation history.
extra.verification_notes: Time balls let ships' navigators check marine chronometers, and the Times Square ball is widely described as descended from them (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_ball).

explanation: Before radio time signals, sailors watched the ball fall at a fixed moment to set their chronometers, and an accurate clock was how they worked out longitude at sea. Greenwich in London has dropped its time ball at 1 pm every day since 1833.

question: In Scotland, the first visitor through your door after midnight on New Year should bring a gift. One classic gift is a lump of something that promises the house will stay warm all year. What is it?
source_excerpt: represent prosperity, food, flavour, warmth for the house, and good cheer

extra.why_interesting: Coal is the last thing you would wrap up as a present. Once players hear what the gift is meant to guarantee, they can reason their way to it and enjoy the odd, practical logic of the tradition.
extra.verification_notes: Coal is the traditional first-footing gift symbolizing warmth for the house; no competing warmth-related gift is listed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-foot).

explanation: The first-footer traditionally brings coal for warmth, and often salt, shortbread or whisky too. The luckiest first-footer of all is said to be a tall, dark-haired man.

question: At midnight, crowds around the world sing "Auld Lang Syne" without knowing what those three Scots words mean. What do they mean, roughly?
source_excerpt: old long since... 'long long ago', 'days gone by', 'times long past', 'old times'

extra.why_interesting: Millions of people sing these three words at midnight every year without knowing what they mean. The answer can be reached by reasoning, since 'auld' sounds like 'old' and the song is about old friends.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia lists 'old times' among the rough renderings of 'Auld Lang Syne' (literally 'old long since'), so the claimed answer is acceptable for a 'roughly' question.

explanation: Word for word it means "old long since", or as we would say, "for old times' sake". So everyone is toasting days gone by and the friends they shared them with.

question: At midnight on New Year's Eve, Buddhist temples in Japan strike their great bell 108 times. According to tradition, what does each strike chase away?
source_excerpt: In Buddhism, there are 108 sins known as kleshas or bonnou (煩悩) in Japanese.

extra.why_interesting: Many people know the bell rings 108 times, but almost nobody knows why that number. It isn't counting hours or days. Each strike banishes one worldly desire, and Buddhist ideas of craving and attachment give players a path to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: The 108 strikes are widely held to dispel the 108 bonnō (earthly desires), so each strike chases away one; the only caveat is that ringing often starts before midnight (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joya_no_Kane).

explanation: Buddhism counts 108 worldly desires that cause human suffering, and each toll clears one away so you can enter the New Year with a clean slate. Many temples strike the last ring just after midnight.

question: One of the first inhabited places on Earth to see the New Year is a Pacific atoll called Christmas Island. Which country does it belong to?
topic: First places to see the New Year
source_excerpt: one of the first inhabited places on Earth to experience New Year's Day

extra.why_interesting: The irony is delightful: the first place on Earth to see the New Year is called Christmas Island. Players often guess New Zealand, Tonga or Samoa as the first country, so naming the right nation takes real knowledge, though the Pacific clue narrows the field.
extra.verification_notes: Kiritimati (Christmas Island), Line Islands, UTC+14, belongs to Kiribati and is the first inhabited place to reach the New Year, as again reported for 2026.

explanation: Christmas Island, or Kiritimati, runs on the world's earliest clock, so its fireworks go off while it's still ten in the morning in London.

question: A New Orleans king cake has a tiny plastic figure baked inside it. What does that figure traditionally represent?
source_excerpt: a small plastic baby symbolizing Jesus is hidden in the king cake

extra.why_interesting: Many people have eaten or seen king cake but never thought about what the little figure stands for. The answer links a party snack directly to the Epiphany story, and the 'you buy the next one' rule is a fun payoff.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's King cake article states the plastic baby in the New Orleans cake symbolizes Jesus.

explanation: The baby stands for the Christ child the Three Kings came to visit. Whoever finds it in their slice is usually expected to bring the next king cake.

question: New Orleans bakeries traditionally start selling king cake on Twelfth Night, January 6th. On which famous day does king cake season end?
source_excerpt: Twelfth Night, January 6th, is the traditional start. ... Mardi Gras closes the season

extra.why_interesting: Players link king cake to Epiphany and assume it is a one-day treat. In fact it is the cake of the whole Carnival season, so a player who knows New Orleans' biggest party can work out the end date.
extra.verification_notes: King cake season traditionally runs from Twelfth Night (Jan 6) through Mardi Gras (Fat Tuesday); no contradicting or newer information found (https://64parishes.org/entry/king-cake).

explanation: King cake belongs to the whole Carnival season, from Epiphany until the last party on Fat Tuesday. Then Lent begins.

question: In Italy, on the night before Epiphany, children get sweets, or coal if they've been naughty, from a kindly old woman who flies on a broomstick. What is her name?
source_excerpt: usually portrayed as a hag riding a broomstick through the air

extra.why_interesting: Players assume Christmas gift-bringers are jolly men like Santa. Italy's Epiphany gift-bringer is a witch-like old woman, which surprises many people. Her name also comes from 'Epifania', so a sharp player can nearly reason it out.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms La Befana visits on Epiphany Eve, rides a broomstick, and gives sweets to good children and coal to bad ones.

explanation: Her name is thought to come from 'Epifania', the Italian word for Epiphany. Legend says she turned down the Three Kings' invitation to join their journey and has been searching for the baby ever since.

question: Legend says the rat won first place in the Chinese zodiac by cheating. It hitched a ride across the river on another animal's back, then jumped off at the finish line. Which animal carried it?
source_excerpt: the Rat rode across the river on the Ox... the Rat pushed the Cat into the water, jumped off the Ox, and reached the Jade Emperor first.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the rat is first in the zodiac but assume it was arbitrary. The answer reveals a trickster story, and the ox's second place makes the 'ride' clue something they can reason out.
extra.verification_notes: In the standard Great Race legend the Rat rides the Ox and jumps off just before the finish; only minor variants (e.g. the dog) differ (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_zodiac).

explanation: The rat leapt off the ox's head at the last moment, which is why the hard-working ox comes second in the zodiac, right behind its passenger.

question: The name December comes from the Latin for 'ten', but it's our twelfth month. In which month did the early Roman year start, so that December really was the tenth?

extra.why_interesting: Everyone says 'December' without noticing it means 'tenth month' while sitting in twelfth place. Players can count backwards from December to find the original starting month.
extra.verification_notes: The early Roman calendar began in March, which made December the tenth month; the account is traditional and partly legendary, but March is the standard answer.

explanation: The Roman year opened in March, which made September the seventh month, October the eighth, November the ninth and December the tenth. January and February were added later.

question: True or false: the year 2100 will be a leap year, with a 29th of February.
source_excerpt: centurial years are leap years only if they are exactly divisible by 400

extra.why_interesting: Most people know the rule 'every four years', and many remember 2000 having a 29 February, so 'True' feels safe. The hidden century rule overturns it.
extra.verification_notes: 2100 is divisible by 100 but not 400, so under the Gregorian rule it is not a leap year (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_year).

explanation: Century years skip the leap day unless they divide by 400. That's why 2000 got a 29 February but 2100 won't, a correction that keeps the calendar in step with the Sun.
